why_use_this: Reach for `BigInt` the moment an integer computation might overflow `i64` -- vāṇी's native integers trap (a hard runtime error) rather than wrap on overflow, and there is no wider native integer type, so exact factorials, large combinatorics, cryptographic-scale numbers, or any computation whose intermediate values you can't bound in advance need this package instead. `BigInt` stores digits as little-endian base-1e9 limbs and is NOT a Copy type (it owns a `Vec<i64>`), so every function takes `ref`/`mut ref BigInt` and returns a fresh `BigInt` by value -- budget for that allocation cost, unlike the Copy-struct sibling libraries ([vani-complex](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-complex), [vani-interval](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-interval)). Despite what the README's "What's included" table currently says ("v0.1.0 -- integers only... Rational numbers... Not started"), this package (now at v0.2.0) actually DOES include a full `Rational` type (`rat_*` functions: construction, arithmetic, comparison, all reduced via `bn_gcd` to lowest terms) built on top of `BigInt` -- reach for `Rational` specifically when you need EXACT fractions with no floating-point rounding at all (`1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3` genuinely equals `1`, not something that merely rounds to it).

math_notes.bn_add: Arbitrary-precision addition: adds magnitudes limb-by-limb with carry propagation (base \( 10^9 \) per limb) when signs match, or subtracts the smaller magnitude from the larger (borrowing the result's sign from whichever operand has greater magnitude) when signs differ -- the standard grade-school algorithm generalized to a base far larger than 10.
math_notes.bn_sub: \( a - b \), computed as \( a + (-b) \) by composing `bn_neg` and `bn_add` rather than a separate subtraction algorithm.
math_notes.bn_mul: Arbitrary-precision multiplication via the schoolbook \( O(n \cdot m) \) algorithm (grade-school long multiplication generalized to base \( 10^9 \) limbs): every limb of \( a \) times every limb of \( b \), accumulated with carries -- not Karatsuba or any faster asymptotic algorithm, the same "simplest correct choice" precedent this ecosystem uses elsewhere.
math_notes.bn_div_mod: Computes both the quotient and remainder of \( a / b \) simultaneously (more efficient than two separate calls, since long division computes both together anyway), TRUNCATING toward zero -- quotient sign is \( \text{sign}(a)\cdot\text{sign}(b) \), remainder sign matches \( a \)'s sign -- deliberately matching vāṇी's native `i64` `/`/`%` semantics rather than mathematical floor division.
math_notes.bn_gcd: The greatest common divisor via the Euclidean algorithm: repeatedly replace \( (a,b) \) with \( (b,\ a \bmod b) \) until \( b=0 \); the surviving \( a \) is \( \gcd(a,b) \) -- the same recurrence Euclid described over two thousand years ago, unchanged. Every `rat_*` constructor calls this to reduce a fraction to lowest terms.
math_notes.bn_pow_i64: \( a^n \) for a non-negative integer exponent \( n \), via exponentiation by repeated squaring (\( O(\log n) \) multiplications instead of \( n-1 \)) -- the arbitrary-precision analog of [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_pow_n`.
math_notes.bn_pow_mod: \( a^n \bmod m \), computed via the same repeated-squaring approach as `bn_pow_i64` but reducing modulo \( m \) after every multiplication -- keeps every intermediate value bounded by \( m \) instead of letting \( a^n \) itself grow to astronomical size before the final reduction, the standard modular-exponentiation technique cryptographic and number-theoretic code relies on.
math_notes.rat_new: Constructs a `Rational` from a numerator/denominator `BigInt` pair, immediately reducing to lowest terms by dividing both by \( \gcd(|num|, |den|) \) (`bn_gcd`) and normalizing the sign onto the numerator so the denominator is always positive -- every `Rational` this package produces is already in this canonical reduced form, so equality comparison (`rat_eq`) can just compare numerator and denominator directly rather than cross-multiplying.
math_notes.rat_add: \( \dfrac{a}{b} + \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad+cb}{bd} \), then reduced to lowest terms by `rat_new` -- the standard cross-multiplication fraction-addition rule, exact (no floating-point rounding) throughout since every intermediate value is a `BigInt`.
math_notes.rat_div: \( \dfrac{a}{b} \div \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad}{bc} \) -- multiply by the reciprocal, reduced by `rat_new`. Undefined (the divisor rational must be nonzero) the same way integer division by zero is undefined.
